title: The Late Berkeley Grad Student Who Solved Two 'Impossible' Theorems
alt_title_1: George Dantzig's 1939 Chalkboard Mistake: How Labels Limit Effort
alt_title_2: Why Calling a Problem 'Unsolved' Stops Smart People From Trying
description_hook: In 1939, UC Berkeley doctoral student George Dantzig arrived late to Professor Jerzy Neyman's statistics class, copied two famous unsolved open theorems off the chalkboard assuming they were homework, and solved both within weeks.

scenes.headline: He Arrived Late and Solved Two Unsolved Theorems
bullets: Walked late into Prof. Jerzy Neyman's 1939 lecture
Copied two open problems off the board as routine homework
scenes.narration: In 1939, UC Berkeley graduate student George Dantzig walked late into Professor Jerzy Neyman's statistics class, copied two famous unsolved theorems off the chalkboard thinking they were homework, and solved both.
scenes.source: George B. Dantzig interview, College Mathematics Journal 17(4) (1986)

scenes.headline: 'A Little Harder Than Usual' Became His PhD Thesis
scenes.stat_label: BOTH PROOFS BOUND DIRECTLY AS DANTZIG'S DISSERTATION
bullets: Apologized to Neyman for taking a few extra days to finish
Six weeks later Neyman submitted one for publication & thesis
scenes.narration: Days later, Dantzig left the proofs on Neyman's desk and apologized because they seemed slightly harder than usual. Six weeks later, an excited Neyman announced those solutions formed Dantzig's doctoral thesis.
scenes.source: George B. Dantzig interview, College Mathematics Journal 17(4) (1986)

scenes.headline: Consensus Labels Shut Down Persistence Early
scenes.left_body: Hears 'nobody can crack this' -> quits at first mental wall
scenes.right_body: Assumes an answer exists -> pushes past friction until solved
scenes.narration: Dantzig later explained that had he arrived on time and heard Neyman introduce those equations as famous unsolved problems, discouragement would have made him quit after the first frustrating afternoon.
scenes.source: George B. Dantzig interview, College Mathematics Journal 17(4) (1986)

scenes.headline: Reframe Scary Bottlenecks as Routine Assignments
scenes.stat_subtext: Mute industry pessimism • 90-min deep block • Assume a clean path exists
scenes.narration: Strip intimidating prestige labels off your hardest engineering or distribution bottleneck, block ninety quiet morning minutes with pen and paper, and work the problem assuming a clean, practical solution is waiting.
scenes.source: Mind & Margin protocol (advice, not a study)

scenes.headline: Stop Mistaking Industry Rumors for Physical Laws
scenes.stat_label: IGNORANCE OF 'IMPOSSIBLE' IS OFTEN AN EDGE
bullets: Test first principles on paper before reading forum cynicism
Treat hard problems like standard Tuesday coursework
scenes.narration: Most capable builders quit before writing line one simply because they treat borrowed industry rumors of impossibility as verified physical laws.
scenes.source: Mind & Margin rule based on Dantzig, CMJ 17(4) (1986)
